_—— 


Annual Report of the Board of Directors 


Metropolitan Plan. 


Your Directors have to present their first report under the 
metropolitan plan of organization. This means that the 
immediate supervision of the detailed work in the Dominion 
Square building is now placed in the hands of a Committee of 
Management, and your Directors are left free to undertake 
the supervision of the branches, and the consideration of the 
needs of the whole city in its relation to this movement. 


Australian Visitation. 


From March until October, the time of your General Secre- 
tary was given to a second tour of visitation of the cities of 
Australia and New Zealand. This visit was followed by Mr. 
Lyman L. Pierce, Secretary at Washington, D.C., going to 
Melbourne for a two years’ service in the Australian field. 
As one result of this visitation they now have five new and 
modern Association buildings in process of erection, and cam- 
paigns for the securing of four additional buildings will be 
carried through this year. This will bring the important 
cities of these islands in the southern hemisphere into line 
with the latest developments of the North American work; 
and the Montreal Association will ever be grateful for the 
part it was permitted to take in_this forward movement. 


Central Building. 


The enlargement of the Central building has been under 
earnest consideration for the past three years, and the neces- 
sity has been most urgent. But difficulties have arisen from 
time to time which prevented your Directors from putting 
through this much needed extension. 

Last November a proposal was made to them to consider 
the sale of the building, and adjoining lot, and after most 
careful consideration they decided to grant an option on the 
building and property for three months. This option was 
afterwards extended until April 1st, 1907, and an option was 


3 


secured on another site which was considered to be suitable 
for the work of Central building in the event of sale. This 
option .expires July 30th. The syndicate failed to take up 
their option for the purchase of the building. 

Your Directors have secured possible plans for the remodel- 
ding of this building with an annex, and also plans for the 
erection of a new building on the present site. They are now ° 
giving most careful consideration to this problem. 

The Committee of Management of the Central building 
will present a detailed report of the past year’s work. It was 
an encouraging fact that the majority of this Committee, 
whom the Board asked to undertake this large responsibility, 
had entered the Association as boys, at the age of 12. The 
Directors appreciate the consecration and earnestness with 
which they have undertaken this work. 


Railroad Branch. 


The Grand Trunk Railroad Branch, at Point St. Charles, 
faced unusual and alarming difficulties. The removal of the 
engineers and firemen to Turcot compelled this Branch not 
only to face a loss of 275 members, but also to rearrange their 
dormitories and general work so as to meet these changed con- 
ditions. In view of these facts your Directors are greatly 
encouraged at the hopeful report which the Branch 
Committee is able to present. 


College Association. 


The College Association, with its handsome and commodi- 
ous new building, fills a most important place in the life of 
the ever-increasing number of students who are attracted to 
MeGill University. In order to bring this work into closer 
affiliation with the general work in the city, Dr. Frank D. 
Adams and Dr. H. M. Tory were added to your Board as 
advisory members. ; 

Northeast End. 


After repeated conferences with a deputation from the 
Fairmount Young Men’s Association, your Board decided to 
unite in taking a lease of the second floor in a new block to 
be erected on the corner of Fairmount and Mance Streets, 
for the establishment of a Branch Association. It is hoped 
this will be ready for November. <A large number of our for- | 
mer members now reside in this section, and have promised 
their hearty co-operation. 

4 


The East End problem has been before your Board for 
three years, but we regret to report that a satisfactory solu- 
tion has not as yet been reached. The district is so widely 
scattered — including the Angus Shop section, the factory 
district at Maisonneuve, and Longue Pointe—that it makes 
it difficult to select a suitable location. The impossibility of 
securing rented quarters makes necessary the erection of a 
special building, which it is estimated would cost $40,000. 
There is great need for a Branch in this section, and the 
promised co-operation of the pastors, churches, and Christian 
workers makes it incumbent upon our Board to respond at 
the earliest possible moment. 


Foreign Work. 


This Association has continued its work among the boys of 
Caleutta, India, through Mr. Chas. 8. Paterson, who is Secre- © 
tary of the Boys’ Branch in that city. Reports from India 
show what an important service Mr. Paterson is rendering in 
laying solid foundation for the future, and also in planning 
for the extension of this special work for boys at other centres 
in India. A larger number of our members should share in 
the financial support of this work, and the Committee invites 
your co-operation. 


Canadian Section of International Committee. 


The Canadian section of the International Committee has 
asked your Directors to grant the time of your Secretary for 
three months in the year for the visitation and development 
of special work in the Canadian field. They have agreed to 
this request provided the service can be rendered so as not to 
interfere seriously with the claims of the local work. 


Conferences. 


The Conferences and Summer Institutes, which are now 
held in the interests of the Association work, are most import- 
ant educational features. This Association has been repre- 
sented at the Canadian Summer School at Lake Couchiching, 
and also at the Silver Bay Institute at Lake George. In the 
opinion of your Directors it is most important that the dele- 
zation should be sent to these Conferences and Institutes. It 
affords our members a larger vision of the movement, and 
keeps them in touch with the later developments. 


a 


el 


Summer Camp. 


Your Directors realize the value of the vacation camp at 
Lae St. Joseph, as a social and recreative feature of the work. 

The Association now owns three Islands, a good Club 
TTouse and equipment, on which there is a debt of $400, part 
of which we hope will be liquidated this year. 

There is a desire expressed to secure another site in a sec- 
tion which would be further removed from civilization, and 
also to retain the present camp. 

The first party for this season leaves on Thursday next to 
spend Victoria Day and the week end. 

The Boys’ Camp opens on June 15th, and the Men’s from 
July 13th to September 30th, 

The privileges of this camp are open to members of all the 


Branches, 
Bequests. 


During the year a bequest of $10,000 was received from 
the executors of the late James Moore-—a life-long friend and 
subseriber, 

Through the death of Miss Orkney in June last, this Asso- 
ciation loses a most interested and valued friend. For many 
years she took a deep personal interest in the progress of the 
work, and was ever ready to co-operate in its advancement. 
By the terms of her will the Association will receive a legacy 
of $10,000, and as residuary legatee the Association will 
receive one-third of the balance when the estate is closed. 

By the will of the late James Cooper, who died July 11, 
1903, this Association is named as residuary legatee, and will 
receive one-third of the balance. This estate has been involved 
in litigation, but we are informed that a settlement wil] likely 
be reached this year, so that the amount due the Association 
will be available. 

To those who have a sense of responsibility for the disposi- 
tion of their money, the choice of channels of benevolence 
is often difficult in order that it may accomplish the largest 
practical good to the community. To such we would respect- 
fully suggest the consideration of The Young Men’s Christian 
Association. . 


Ist. Because it is an incorporated body owning large prop- 
erty interests in the city, which must ever be administered by 
Christian business men, representing the various religious 
denominations. 


2nd. Because, while independent in action, it is closely 
related by affiliation and supervision to one of the largest 
organizations on this continent, and throughout the world; 
in promoting the highest interests of youth and manhood, and 
because it is absolutely unselfish in its line of effort, and 
includes in its objective all young men, irrespective of class 
or creed. 


3rd. Because of economy of administration from the fact 
that this work is so largely preventive in its plan, and also 
from the fact that money operates at the same time on so 
many lines, the moral, educational, physical, and social wel- 
fare of boys and men. 


4th. Because of the fact that its benefits extend to the entire 
city, and to all classes of young men by reason of its 
Branches. 


5th. Because it affords a wide diversity of objects to which 
funds may be applied according to the inclination of the 
donor, viz., towards the erection of buildings, the endowment 
of the work, for libraries, for evening educational classes for 
commercial and mechanical young men, for moral and 
religious teaching, and for the extension of the work through- 
out the city. 


6th. Because in the past five years such a large number of 
the clear-headed business men, and thoughtful far-seeing 
women on this continent have placed large sums of money 
either by gift or bequest at the disposal of this movement, 
and this has been done in many cases after careful investiga- 
tion of its methods and plans of work. 


7th. Because this City of Montreal has the honor of being 
the birthplace of this organization on the North American 
Continent, and therefore it should keep in the front rank of 
leadership, and because of the service which it has rendered 
to this community in the development of young men into 
broad-minded and aggressive Christian citizenship. 


In considering the work for the coming year your Direc- 
tors will aim to conserve the well-established plans on which 
we are now working, and also reach out on the following 
lines: 

ist. For an enlarged financial constituency to meet the 
needs of an expanding work. An increasing number of our 
members should be given an opportunity and encouraged to 


‘ 


make a voluntary contribution in addition to their member- 
ship fee. 


2nd. The extension of work for boys in the formation and 
management of clubs in districts beyond the reach of the 
Branches. 


3rd: The extension of our religious work into shops, the 
establishment of home and district Bible classes, and perfect- 
ing the organization of our religious work. 


4th. The giving of greater attention to the thousands of 
young men who come to our land as immigrants. 


5th. The securing of a Christian summer home within half 
an hour’s ride of Montreal at the water side, owned and con- 
trolled by the Association, where young men earning small 
salaries could find a congenial summer home. When estab- 
lished this would be self-supporting. 


6th. The securing of relief from the following obligations: 
A mortgage of $12,000 on the lots adjoining the Central 
building; a debt of $9,000 incurred in new construction and 
equipment as a result of the fire at the Central building, above 
the amount received from insurance; $9,000 mortgage on the 
Railroad building at Point St. Charles; and $2,400 debt on 
current expenses at the Railroad Branch. 


Your Directors are thankful to be able to report all bills 
paid on current expenses on their own budget, as well of 
those of the Branches for the past year, and they desire to 
thank each one who by gift or personal service has in any way 
made possible this larger service on behalf of the men and 
boys of our city. 

They also wish to record their deep sense of gratitude to 
God for the continued favor and blessing which He hag so 
freely granted in answer to the united prayers and efforts of 
the workers. 


JOHN W. ROSS, 


President. 


D. A. BUDGE, 
General Secretary.

Annual Report of Committee of 
Management, Dominion Square Buildings. 


On May Ist, 1906, the Board of Directors inaugurated the Metro- 
politan plan, by which the supervision of the work in the Dominion 
Square Building was entrusted to a Committee of Management 
appointed by the Board. This Committee accepted the task with a 
deep sense of responsibility. They are grateful to God for the measure 
of success which has been attained. 


MEMBERSHIP. 


The total membership on April 30th, 1907, was 2,405. The total 
receipts from fees were $9,742.25, a gain of $1,023.85 over last yeur.

RELIGIOUS. 


The Religious Meetings and Bible Classes have been held regularly, 
with encouraging results. 


No. Sessions. Total Att. Average 
Saturday Night Meeting.. .. .. . . 52 2,552 50 
Meon’s' Mécting< 5." 40k be dae 31 4,718 152 
Sunday Afternoon Bible Class.. .. 46 1,996 43 


The Men’s Meeting was held from September 29th to April 30th. 
During April this meeting co-operated with the Torrey evangelistic 
movement. Amongst the prominent speakers from a distance were: 
Mr. Fred. B. Smith, of New York; Rev. Principal Gordon, of Queen’s 
University; Rev. Bradford Williams, of Brooklyn, N.Y.; Rev. Chas. A. 
Eaton, of Cleveland, Ohio, and Dr. Lyman B, Sperry, of Oberlin, Ohio. 

The Tuesday Evening Bible Classes were continued during the 
summer months with good results. In the fall the classes were 
reorganized and enlarged. The following leaders took part: Messrs. 
J. E. Merritt, J. Stuart Jamieson, W. S. Williamson, R. L. Charlton, 
E. J. Figgis, D. A. Budge, and C. K. Calhoun. 

The Sunday Morning Services have been held at the Western 
Hospital, conducted by Mr. W. S. Leslie and Mr. Jas. A. Ogilvy, Jr., 
assisted by other members of the Association staff. 

During the summer months an informal song service was held on 
the steps of the Association Building on Sunday evenings after church. 
Large crowds of people on the square were attracted. 

This year the entire time of one member of the staff will be 
devoted to this work. ~ 


FOREIGN. 


The Foreign Work Committee has cared for the fund by which 
Mr. Charles 8. Paterson carries on a work for Hindoo boys in Caleutta, 
India. 

Mr. W. Y. King, Treasurer of the fund, reports:

At the annual conference of our Foreign Work on January 31st, 
Mr. E. T. Colton, of New York, was the speaker. A large part of the 
fund for the current year was repledged, and the Committee will 
secure the balance. 


11 


EMPLOYMENT, INFORMATION, AND RELIEF. 


From 9 to 10.30 a.m. young men have been counselled in reference 
to employment. The majority of men applying have been strangers 
in the city. 

Hundreds of young men have been assisted to boarding houses, 
Selita in their difficulties, and where possible, aided in their 
distress, 


SOCTAL. 


A short Entertainment Course, the New Year’s Reception, infor- 
mal social evenings, and the Strangers’ Tea, at which 400 young men 
who had newly arrived from different countries were welcomed, was 
held during the fall and winter. 

The Association Lunch Room was opened October ist. It’ has 
been appreciated by the men rooming in the building, and also proves 
a strong social feature with the membership. There was a credit 
balance of $260.16 on the seven months’ operation. 


EDUCATIONAL. 


Commencing September 24th, classes for employed men were con- 
dueted in Arithmetic, Composition, Business Correspondence, Book- 
keeping, Shorthand, Typewriting, Penmanship, French, German, 
Accountaney, Mechanical Drawing, Architectural Drawing, Electricity, 
Electrical Engineering, Insurance, Steam Engineering, Shop Mathe- 
matics, Matriculation. Twenty-nine classes met each week. The work 
for the boys was taken up in a group course. Arithmetic, Spelling, 
Penmanship, History, and Geography were taught. The class met 
twice each week. 

The individual enrolment was 567, and the class enrolment 709, 
the total attendance being 12,946. 

The total amount received in fees was $2,632.10, as against 
$2,156.00 last year, a gain of $476.10. 

Total expenses for the year $2,853.80. Last year $2,308.45, an 
increase of $545.35 

One hundred and sixty-four ‘students wrote on fifteen subjects 
in the examinations conducted by the International Committee. Of 
these 101 were marked over 75% by the local examiners. Twelve men 
will write on the International examinations in June, and nine will 
write on the Matriculation examinations. 

The insurance class was a new feature, in which eight men 
studied. Of these, four wrote on the examinations set by the Insur- 
ance Institute. Another new and successful feature is the Boys’ Own 
Science Club, which meets weekly in charge of the Educational 
Secretary. :

The Debating Club met every Monday evening. Besides the 
general debates and diseussions among the members, and a mock trial, 
two debates were held with other societies, and two dinners given. The 
membership is 30. 

A series of Practical Talks was arranged as follows: 


I.—‘‘Four Tlustrated Lectures on Ships and Ship Building,’’ by 
Mr. A. J. C. Robertson. 

II.—‘‘ Three Talks on Tllumination,’’ by Mr. Cagney; ‘‘ Electric 
Motors,’’ by Mr. Kenneth Drinkwater; and ‘‘ Electrical Construction 
and Transmission,’’ by Mr. R. F. Howard. 

TII.—On “« Barthquakes,”’ by Dr. F. D. Adams, McGill Univer- 
ity; on ‘‘Stock-broking,’’ by Mr. J. Pitblado; on ‘‘The Notarial 
@ rofession, ”’ by Mr. Geo. R. Lighthall. 

The following series of Practical Talks were given under the, 
auspices of the Montreal Debating Club: 

‘*Organized Charity,’’ by. Mr. Richard H. Lane; ‘‘The Eduea- 
tional System in the Province of Quebee,’’? by Rey. Principal Shaw; 
‘The Transportation Problem of Montreal,’’ by Mr. Robt. Bickerdike, 
M.P.; ‘‘Edueation,’’ by Mr. Godfroi Langlois; “‘Single Tax,’’ by 
Mr. Henry Timmis.

READING ROOM AND LIBRARY, 


The Library contains 4,975 volumes. One hundred and eighty- 
five have been added during the year. Seven hundred and ninety-six 
members are using its privileges, and 8,724 books have been issued.

dred and fifty-five different men and boys registered in the classes, as 
compared with 783 last year; 407 passed the physical and medical 
examinations. A statement of attendance is given as follows:

Dr. R. C. Paterson also conducted a successful class in ‘‘ First 
Aid to the Injured’ on Tuesday evenings. 

A new feature this year was the formation of a Sunday School 
Athletic League to co-operate with the Sunday Schools in the develop-

The various clubs report as follows: 

The Bowling Club won the championship of an independent 
league, and have kept up their reputation of winning every home game 
since December, 1903. They closed the s ith a eredit balance 
of $61.23. 

The Foot lub had a total me

The Snowshoe Club had a total membership of 85, an increase of 
17 over last year.  ] 

The Basketball Club has three Weams in the Senior League and 
four in the Intermediate, with the usual championship games. 

The Tennis Club had a membership of 47. The Club won the 
championship of the City League, and two members won the champion- 
ship of the doubles for the Province of Quebec. The Club had a 
credit balance of $7.41. 

The Baseball and Harrier Clubs found difficulty in maintaining 
the interest owing to adverse conditions,

Report of Women’s Auxillary. 


The work of the Auxiliary has been administered by six Com- 
mittees, all of whom have been earnest and enthusiastic in carrying out 
the part allotted to them. 

The Social Committee, under the leadership of Mrs. Budge, has 
done most efficient work in assisting at the banquets, socials, and 
receptions. ‘he principal functions have been the Committeemen’s 
Tea, New Year’s Reception, Reception tendered Mr. N. H. Holmes, of 
New Zealand, and the Physical Department Banquet on April 4th. 
They have also rendered most helpful service to the Gymnasium Men’s 
Bible Class and the Strangers’ Tea each Sunday afternoon. 

The Furnishing Committee expended $717.00 in securing rugs, cur- 
tains, shades, and portieres for the Association rooms. 

The Flower Committee, under Mrs. MeKergow, have supplied 
flowers to twenty-eight sick young men during the year. This has 
been a most helpful service, and many grateful letters have been 
received from young men. 

The Finance Committee has secured 142 subscribers now, and 
$250.00 has been received during the past year, and they are planning 
for larger things. 

The Junior Committee, under the leadership of Mrs. John W. Ross, 
@as rendered splendid service to the boys’ work, co-operating with them 
in all their social functions, such as luncheons, teas, suppers, sleigh 
drives, ete. 

They also provided curtains and carpets for furnishing the boys’ 
rooms. 

A reception was held in February for the parents and friends, and 
was highly successful. 7 

Your Committee regret to report the loss. by death of one of our 
most earnest kers, Mrs. Robert Henderson. Also the removal from 
the city of Mrs. C. W. Brown. We also regret to report that we are 
losing, through ill-health, our efficient Treasurer, Mrs. E. B. Busteed. 


President—Mrs. Lemuel Cushing. 

Ist Vice-President—Mrs. William Tees. 

2nd Vice-President—Mrs. Henry Birks. 

Recording Seeretary—Mrs. W. Godbee Brown. 
Corresponding Seeretary—Miss Currie. 
Treasurer—Mrs. J. Ritchie Bell.

Convener Junior Committee—Mrs. Arthur Paterson. 
Convener Furnishing Committee—Mrs. W. A. Gandle. 
Convener Finance Committee—Mrs. C. T. Williams, 
Convener Flower Committee—Mrs. John MeKergow. 
Convener Nominating Committee—Mrs. Geo. Lamb.

Railroad Young Men’s Christian Association 
Point St. Charles 


On the 30th of April we closed the third year of the work of the 
Railroad Department of the Young Men’s Christian Association in the 
new building. 

At the commencement of the year your Committee was called upon 
to face an almost entirely new situation with regard to one of the 
principal sources of revenue, namely, the rest rooms. The road men 
had all been transferred to Turcot, hence the problem of rearranging 
and furnishing the rooms that they might be suitable for permanent 
use by shop and office men. About $300.00 was expended, with the 
result that while we had 20 men as regular roomers the first of the 
year, we now have 60. 

The religious work has been well sustained. There were 39 dif- 
ferent speakers at the Sunday afternoon meetings. These meetings 
are now for men only. The total attendance at same was 1.965, an 
average of 38. There were also held during the season 30 Saturday 
night meetings, six noon-day meetings, and 63 Bible Class sessions. 
A ‘‘Home Circle’? band of men has been formed for the purpose of 
visiting homes needing help, with the object of brightening and making 
same happier. 

Among the social features of the Association the work of the 
Bowling Committee is worthy of special attention. Another special 
feature has been the introduction of two pool tables. The results have 
entirely justified the views of the Committee. The Fall opening and 
Members’ Rally, also the New Year’s Day Reception, were both very 
successful. 

The work of the Physical Department of the Association has been 
placed upon a successful basis. Last fall we engaged as Physical 
Instructor, Mr. F. A. Erfling, and the work has made substantial 
progress. Through the kindness of the Grand Trunk the Association 
has been granted the use of a field for athletic purposes. This will be 
a valuable asset for this department. 

The increased use of the rooms accounts for the increased 
restaurant business, which has more than doubled since the opening 
of the year. : 

An important feature has been the starting of work for boys. 
We now take in a limited number of school boys from 12 to 15, and a 
limited number of working boys from 15 to 18. 

The Association has sustained the loss of two of its most active 
members, viz: Thos. M. Hamilton and Russell W. Parr. Both of 
these young men met their death by accident while in the performance 
of their duty. ‘ 

The Committee desires to acknowledge and thank the city Board 
of Directors for tHeir generous and unfailing support in all that has 
pertained to the work of the Association during the year.
